feedback: If the plate is all one food, ask: which food groups are missing, and which nutrient jobs (energy, growth material, protection) may now go short? Point back to the empty segments.

If portions are equal across all groups, prompt: the guide does not use equal shares — with the Eatwell Guide, fruit/veg and starchy foods are the biggest parts and oils/spreads tiny — adjust the amounts, not just which foods are present.
If a treat is placed into a main group, note that high fat/sugar foods sit outside the main groups and are eaten less often.
Praise correct reasoning that names a food's food group and the nutrients it supplies, not just that a food 'is healthy'.
activities.intendedInsight: Balance is not 'a bit of everything equally' — it is the right amounts of each food group, with (in the Eatwell Guide) fruit/veg and starchy foods making up most of the plate and treats only occasional; and balance is judged over a day or week, not at every single meal.
learnerActions: Collect real or pictured everyday foods the child actually eats, then sort each into the food groups of a local healthy-eating guide (Eatwell: fruit and vegetables; starchy carbohydrates; proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads, with treats outside the main groups — or the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating's five food groups).

Arrange foods onto a plate divided into the guide's food-group proportions (with Eatwell, fruit/veg and starchy foods fill the largest areas, protein and dairy smaller areas, oils/spreads a tiny area, and sugary/fatty treats sit off to the side as occasional).
Deliberately try an unbalanced plate — a mountain of chips only, or nothing but fruit — and describe which food groups are missing and which nutrient jobs may not be covered.

As each food is placed, say its food group and one main nutrient it supplies and what that nutrient does (e.g. bread: starchy food, supplies carbohydrate for energy; chicken: protein food, supplies protein for growth and repair), noting that most foods supply several nutrients.
Look across a whole day or week and check whether one wobbly meal is evened out by the others.
activities.title: Build a balanced plate

feedback: If a sandwich is forced into a single group, ask what the bread, filling and spread each contribute.
Confirm when a learner explains that milk sits in one food group (dairy and alternatives) yet supplies several nutrients, such as protein, fat and calcium.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixed dishes combine foods from several food groups, and most foods supply several nutrients, so neither classification is one-to-one.
learnerActions: Classify everyday foods into the guide's food-group bins, including a dedicated 'mixed foods' bin.
Break down mixed dishes — a pizza, a sandwich — into the food groups their ingredients come from, naming each part, and list the several nutrients a single food such as a glass of milk supplies.
Discuss why a mixed dish draws on several food groups, and why even a single food supplies several nutrients.
activities.title: Sort mixed foods

feedback: If a learner says fat should be avoided completely, explain the body needs some fat for energy, warmth and storage; the issue is amount and balance, not cutting out a whole nutrient.
If a learner endorses Sam's oranges/vitamin-tablet plan, point out vitamins don't supply energy or build muscle — identify the carbohydrate source for energy and the protein source for growth.
If treats are called forbidden, reframe: occasional treats can fit within an overall balance.
Reward answers that reject 'healthy = strong' reasoning and correctly assign carbohydrates to energy and protein to growth.
activities.intendedInsight: No single food or nutrient is simply 'bad' or 'banned' — even fats are needed for energy, warmth and storage; it is the overall balance and amount across a day or week that matters, and each nutrient must be matched to the job it actually does.
learnerActions: Pose 'is X bad for me?' questions and answer using nutrient jobs and overall balance rather than a 'good food / bad food' verdict.

Consider Sam's claim that fat is always bad and should be avoided completely — explain why the body still needs some fat (for energy, warmth and storage) and that it is the amount and balance that matter, not banning a whole nutrient.

Work through the swimmer example: Sam says he'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets because 'vitamins give you energy and make you strong' — decide whether to agree and explain what he should eat for energy (carbohydrates: bread, pasta, rice) and for building muscle (protein: chicken, fish, eggs, beans), and why each helps.
Reason about what might go wrong on race day if someone ate only protein and no carbohydrates, and why we still need vitamins regularly in our food even though they give no energy.
activities.title: Myth-busting: is this food bad for me?
